PART TEN
Joy & Gratitude
CHAPTER 86
Making Room for Gratitude
Some gifts are easy to name, such as help with a difficulty you
could not manage alone. Others have become so familiar that
you rarely stop over them. A person keeps showing up, or a skill
someone taught you continues to help you through the day.
Gratitude can begin when you give one of these things your
attention. What have you received? Why does it matter to you?
You do not need a remarkable event before there is something
worth bringing to God in thanks.
You may also have days when thankfulness comes easily. Let the
prayer be simple then. You are allowed to enjoy something good
and tell Him you are glad.
The man who returns
Luke 17 describes Jesus entering a village while traveling toward
Jerusalem. Ten men with leprosy stand at a distance and call to
Him for mercy. Jesus tells them to show themselves to the
priests. As they go, they are cleansed.
One of the men sees that he has been healed and returns,
praising God aloud. He falls at Jesus' feet and gives thanks. Luke
identifies him as a Samaritan. Jesus asks where the other nine

407
are and draws attention to this foreigner returning to give glory
to God.
He recognizes what he has received and comes back to the One
who helped him. Consider a need of your own that has been met.
Have you had time to give thanks, or has your attention already
moved elsewhere?
You might return to a prayer you once made and say thank you
for the help that followed. Or you may notice a kindness that you
never specifically requested. God can be thanked for good you
did not think to put on a list of needs.
Give thanks with a reason
Psalm 100 invites worshipers into thanksgiving:
Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise;
give thanks to Him and bless His name.
Psalm 100:4, Berean Standard Bible
The next verse gives a reason: the Lord is good, His loving
devotion endures, and His faithfulness continues through
generations. Thanksgiving is directed toward His character as
well as what a person has recently received.
This can deepen a brief prayer. You might thank God for a
friend's patience and ask to learn that patience yourself. You
might give thanks for provision and remember the work of
those through whom it came. Notice the particular good before
turning it into a general statement about being blessed.
James 1:17 speaks of good gifts coming from the Father, whose
goodness does not shift. The surrounding verses distinguish His
giving from temptation and the workings of sinful desire.
Gratitude can direct attention toward His goodness without
requiring you to call every event good.

408
Let appreciation reach the person involved
Consider someone whose contribution you have come to expect.
A direct thank-you can name what you noticed and why it
helped. “You stayed to listen when I was finding it difficult to
explain” says more than a compliment they cannot connect to
anything they did.
Keep the words proportionate and true. The person may have
offered something small that mattered greatly at the time. You
can appreciate that gift without making them responsible for
continuing it indefinitely.
Where there is an opportunity to express thanks, choose a form
that suits the relationship. It may be a conversation, a short
message, or care offered in return when they need it. Receiving
help gratefully includes respecting what the other person can
freely give.
You can also acknowledge good work by someone you barely
know. A few words about their careful explanation or patient
response can let them know that you noticed.
Give gratitude room beside the rest of life
First Thessalonians 5:16–18 places rejoicing, prayer, and
thanksgiving within the community's life. The instruction is to
give thanks in every circumstance. It does not require approval
of cruelty or a cheerful explanation for loss. The same passage's
wider setting calls for encouraging the fainthearted and helping
the weak.
If life is difficult, you may be able to name one kindness within
it. You may also need someone to hear what hurts before you can
do that. Gratitude offered freely can coexist with a request for
change. It should not be demanded as proof that your suffering
has become acceptable.
On an ordinary day, try pausing over something you would
otherwise pass by. Stay with it long enough to say what you

409
appreciate. If you want to remember it later, a note, an object, or
a conversation may help. Choose what serves you; there is no
required record to complete.
Over time, this attention may also prompt a question about how
you use what you receive. Is there something you can share,
protect, or care for more thoughtfully? Thanksgiving can lead
into a response suited to the gift and your circumstances.
If someone you care about is grateful
Give them room to describe what they appreciate. Ask a
question that lets them enjoy telling you, and allow their
experience to remain the subject for a while. You may notice the
goodness of something you had taken for granted too.
If they thank you, receive the words simply. You need not
dismiss the help as nothing or turn the moment into an account
of how much you sacrificed. Their thanks can be heard without
creating a debt between you.
For reflection
• What have you received recently that you would like to name
before God?
• Whose contribution has become familiar enough that you
seldom acknowledge it?
• Is there a way to care for or share something you are grateful to
have?

410
Prayer
Father, thank You for the good I have received, including what I
have been too hurried to notice. Help me appreciate the people
through whom care has come. Let my thanks be specific and honest,
and guide me in using what You have given with care. Amen.
For further reading: Luke 17:11–19; Psalm 100; James 1:13–18; 1 Thessalonians 5:14–22.
Read also: When There Is Good News to Celebrate (p. 411), Remembering an
Answered Prayer (p. 424), Learning to Give (p. 138).
